qs.q: A 50-year-old man with septic shock secondary to a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm remains hypotensive despite initial balanced crystalloid resuscitation and correction of his surgical bleeding source. According to ICU management guidelines, what is the first-line vasoactive agent of choice to restore perfusion pressure?
qs.e: Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor of choice in septic and vasodilatory shock when fluid resuscitation fails to restore adequate mean arterial pressure. Dobutamine is reserved as an inotrope if myocardial dysfunction is present.

qs.q: A 72-year-old man undergoes an open repair of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm within two hours of presentation. How is this operation classified according to its surgical urgency?
qs.e: Emergency operations are indicated immediately within hours for life-threatening conditions such as a ruptured aneurysm or bowel perforation. Urgent procedures are typically performed within days for conditions like an obstructed bowel.

exam: What bedside findings would make you suspect a ruptured AAA and what is your immediate management? — Identify pulsatile mass, hypotension, back pain; initiate permissive hypotension, arrange urgent surgery.

How does the management of a 5 cm asymptomatic AAA differ in a low‑resource hospital versus a tertiary centre? — Surveillance with ultrasound vs. referral for EVAR if available; discuss open repair feasibility.
Explain why a mycotic aneurysm requires antibiotics before any surgical repair. — Infection weakens wall; antibiotics reduce sepsis risk and improve graft survival.
A patient with HIV presents with a 4.5 cm AAA; what extra considerations affect timing of repair? — CD4 count, opportunistic infection risk, drug interactions with antiretrovirals.
Why are β‑blockers preferred over calcium‑channel blockers for blood‑pressure control in AAA? — β‑blockers reduce heart rate and shear stress more effectively; CCBs may cause reflex tachycardia.

Interpret an ultrasound report showing an AAA of 5.2 cm with a mural thrombus. What are the next steps? — Near threshold for repair; assess growth trend, consider elective open repair if symptomatic or rapid growth.
What complications should you monitor for after open AAA repair in a setting without ICU facilities? — Bleeding, graft infection, renal failure, limb ischemia; plan early mobilization and wound care.

How would you differentiate a retroperitoneal haematoma from a ruptured AAA on bedside exam? — AAA gives a palpable pulsatile mass; haematoma is non‑pulsatile, often tender, and may shift with position.
ai.title: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: An abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a focal dilation of the infrarenal aorta that can rupture catastrophically. Diagnosis relies on imaging, risk assessment uses size and symptoms, and management balances surveillance with repair, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: ≥3 cm diameter on any imaging modality
Rapid growth >0.5 cm in 6 months suggests instability
sections.p: A focal, permanent enlargement of the abdominal aorta to ≥3 cm or ≥50 % above normal diameter. Diagnosis is confirmed by imaging that shows the aortic wall bulge.

t.b: Is there an aneurysm and what is its size? – Gives diameter; portable and cheap, ideal where CT is unavailable.
What is the exact anatomy and suitability for endovascular repair? – Provides precise measurements; if unavailable, rely on ultrasound + plain X‑ray for calcification.
Can calcified aortic wall be seen when no advanced imaging? – May show calcified rim; not reliable for size.

b: Small: 3–4 cm, low rupture risk; surveillance.
Medium: 4–5.5 cm, consider repair if rapid growth or comorbidities.
Large: >5.5 cm or symptomatic, urgent repair.
sections.p: Staging is based on maximal diameter and symptom status, guiding urgency of repair.

b: Atherosclerotic degeneration (most common worldwide).
Mycotic aneurysm from Salmonella, Staphylococcus, or HIV‑related opportunists.
Syphilitic aortitis (rare, but still seen).
Trauma or iatrogenic injury.
Genetic connective‑tissue disorders (e.g., Marfan) – less common locally.
sections.p: AAA is multifactorial; atherosclerosis dominates, but infections and local factors matter in East Africa.

b: Pulsatile abdominal mass, best felt mid‑line, 1–2 cm above umbilicus.
Deep, constant back or flank pain radiating to groin.
Acute abdominal pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile mass → ruptured AAA.
Absence of femoral pulses may indicate distal embolisation or rupture.
sections.p: Many AAAs are silent; when symptomatic they give clues to size or impending rupture.

b: Baseline CBC, renal function, and type & screen before surgery.
Blood group and cross‑match for possible transfusion.
sections.p: Imaging confirms size, morphology and suitability for repair; labs guide peri‑operative care.

t.b: Is the patient fit for contrast CT? – Normal → proceed; elevated → consider non‑contrast CT or ultrasound.
Will massive transfusion be needed if rupture occurs? – Ensures blood is ready.

b: Sudden severe abdominal or back pain.
Hypotension with tachycardia.
New onset abdominal bruit or loss of femoral pulses.
Rapid aneurysm growth on serial imaging.
sections.p: Prompt recognition of impending rupture saves lives.

b: Smoking cessation – reduces expansion rate.
Blood pressure control with β‑blockers or ACE‑inhibitors; avoid excessive vasodilation that may mask rupture signs.
Statins for atherosclerotic disease.
Elective repair: open surgical grafting (most common in low‑resource settings) or endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) if expertise/equipment exist.
Rupture: immediate resuscitation, permissive hypotension (SBP 80–90 mmHg), rapid transfer to operating theatre.
sections.p: Treat the aneurysm, control risk factors, and prepare for repair when indicated.

b: Ultrasound every 6 months for 3–4 cm AAAs; yearly for 4–5 cm if stable.
Control hypertension (<130/80 mmHg).
Annual lipid profile; treat dyslipidaemia.
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce systemic inflammation.
sections.p: Surveillance prevents missed growth; lifestyle measures limit new aneurysm formation.

b: Pancreatic pseudocyst – non‑pulsatile, associated with pancreatitis.
Renal tumour – flank mass, no pulsation, may have hematuria.
Retroperitoneal sarcoma – firm, non‑pulsatile, slower growth.
sections.p: Other abdominal masses can mimic a pulsatile AAA.

b: Normal abdominal X‑ray does not exclude an aneurysm; rely on ultrasound/CT.
Mildly elevated creatinine may be chronic; assess trend before denying contrast CT.
sections.p: Certain findings may give false reassurance.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal or back pain with hypotension
